title: MCP in 2026: Stateless Core, Enterprise Auth & Ecosystem Growth
content:
## Overview

The Model Context Protocol (MCP), introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, has grown from a niche standard into infrastructure most major AI-tool vendors now support. This page tracks how the protocol itself and its ecosystem evolved through 2026, building on the fundamentals covered in "Tool Use & Agents."

---

## The 2026 Roadmap

Published March 9, 2026, the MCP roadmap organized the year's protocol work around four themes:

1. **Transport scalability** — moving beyond the original stdio/SSE model toward infrastructure that scales on ordinary HTTP
2. **Agent communication** — standardizing how agents (not just clients and servers) coordinate
3. **Governance maturation** — a formal process for evolving the spec without breaking existing integrations
4. **Enterprise readiness** — authorization and access control suitable for large organizations

---

## The 2026-07-28 Release Candidate

The release candidate dated 2026-07-28 is described as the largest revision of the protocol since its launch. Headline changes:

- **Stateless core** — the base protocol no longer requires a server to hold session state between requests, letting MCP servers scale on standard HTTP infrastructure (load balancers, autoscaling groups) the way REST APIs do, instead of pinning clients to long-lived stateful connections.
- **MCP Apps extension** — allows servers to return server-rendered UI, not just structured data or text, so a tool call can hand back an interactive surface rather than only JSON.
- **Tasks extension** — first-class support for long-running work: a tool call can return a task handle immediately and let the client poll or subscribe for completion, instead of holding the connection open for slow operations.
- **Authorization aligned with OAuth/OIDC** — brings MCP's auth flow closer to standards enterprises already run, rather than a bespoke scheme.
- **Formal deprecation policy** — the protocol can now evolve on a defined schedule instead of breaking integrations with undocumented changes.

---

## Enterprise-Managed Authorization (Stable)

The Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) extension reached stable status in 2026, giving organizations a centralized way to gate MCP server access through their existing identity provider. The stated goal is to replace **per-server consent prompts** with a zero-touch flow: a user signs in once, and access to every approved server follows automatically, rather than re-approving each server individually.

---

## Ecosystem Growth

The server ecosystem scaled dramatically in under a year and a half:

| Point in time | Servers available |
|---|---|
| November 2024 (launch) | ~100 |
| March 2026 (Glama registry) | 19,831+ |

Major platforms now ship official MCP servers or endpoints, including GitHub, Slack, Notion, Stripe, Salesforce, and — as of June 30, 2026 — **X**, which launched an MCP server to make its platform easier for AI tools to query and act on directly.

---

## Why It Won

MCP's core pitch — one integration works with any MCP-compatible client — held up against competing proprietary tool-connection formats because it decoupled the tool-builder from the agent-framework. A GitHub MCP server built for one client (e.g. Claude Code) works unmodified with any other MCP host, which is the same dynamic documented in the original Tool Use & Agents page, just at much larger scale now that tens of thousands of servers exist.

---

## Practical Implication

For anyone building or consuming MCP servers today: expect the stateless-core and Tasks-extension changes to matter most for long-running tool calls (the kind that previously required awkward polling workarounds or kept a connection open), and expect EMA adoption to matter most in enterprise deployments where per-server consent prompts had become an onboarding bottleneck.
